rv.q: Manzi’s is a play about disenfranchisement, and how humans seek community in strange and unexpected places.
In texture, the piece (translated by William Gregory) feels akin to a Caryl Churchill play, with its teasing obliqueness and surprising, dark shafts of humour.
It might, though, leave several audience members scratching their heads.
More often, the director Sam Pritchard allows it to fall into static exchanges where, on Rosie Elnile’s functional set, there is little to nourish the eye.
Every element of this performance works together beautifully; the set is understated, but it becomes more and more layered as the play unfolds.

cn.t: Manzi's English-language debut earns praise for its sharp wit and exploration of violence and community across fragmented Latin American scenes, though some find the ambitious scope uneven in execution.
